name: Nominalism about universals ('Of General Terms')
plain_explanation: Only particular, individual things actually exist in the world. When we use a general word like 'man,' we are not naming some extra abstract thing that all men share -- we are using one particular idea in our minds as a label that applies to many similar particulars.
precise_definition: All things that exist are particulars; general ideas (such as 'man') are applicable to many particulars, but in their own being, as ideas in the mind, they are just as particular as anything else that exists -- their generality consists solely in their applicability to many things.
why_it_mattered: This 'extreme nominalist position,' extended in Book III's attack on the scholastic doctrine of real 'essence,' cleared away what Russell calls 'metaphysical lumber': it treats species boundaries as made by human classification rather than as fixed in nature, anticipating (though not developing) evolutionary ways of thinking later vindicated by Darwin.
historical_origin: Book III of the Essay, Chapter III ('Of General Terms') and Chapter VI ('Of the Names of Substances').
examples: The general idea 'man' applying to many particular men
Monstrosities/borderline cases used by Locke to show species boundaries are man-made, not natural facts
The scholastic debate over whether the 'essence' of body is extension alone or extension plus solidity, which Locke treats as merely verbal
competing_positions: The scholastic doctrine of real essences fixed in nature
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes this point of view was not generally accepted until Darwin persuaded people to think in terms of gradual, continuous change rather than fixed species.
